summary: Mixed-workload priority starvation causing elevated 5xx rate and runtime restarts for Nimbus Analytics
description:
Issue summary:
Customer Nimbus Analytics reported a sustained increase in 5xx responses (predominantly 502/503) on their mixed workload routes (chat + embedding bulk upload) beginning 2026-03-10 02:00 UTC. The elevated error rate correlated with a pattern of short-chat sessions interleaved with large embedding uploads from the same tenant.

Impact:
- Customer saw ~12% overall error rate on their ingestion and chat endpoints for ~90 minutes, causing failed ingestion jobs and degraded UX.
- Several upstream serving-runtime processes restarted with OOM-like termination logs; requests for the tenant repeatedly failed until runtime pods were recycled.
- Business impact: ingestion backfill jobs aborted; customer success escalated to enterprise support.

Environment:
- Redwood hosted (prod - us-east-1)
- Tenant: Nimbus Analytics (enterprise, dedicated routing)
- Routes affected: /v1/chat/stream (streaming), /v1/embeddings/upload (batch)
- Models serving: text-embed-2-large (batch), redwood-chat-v1 (streaming)

Timeline & reproduction steps observed by Support:
1) 2026-03-10 01:58 UTC - first anomaly detected by SLO alerting: 5xx rate > 5% for tenant routes.
2) 02:00-02:20 UTC - spikes of short chat sessions (~100-300ms) interleaving with large embedding multipart uploads.
3) 02:21 UTC - several runtime pods handling the tenant showed abrupt exits and restart loops.
4) 02:45 UTC - apigw backpressure increased, connection queue depth rose and further request failures observed.
5) 03:20 UTC - mitigations (rate-limit tenant burst, re-route heavy uploads to lower-priority path) applied; error rate began to decline.

Steps to reproduce (lab):
- From a tenant-shared VM, simulate 30 concurrent tiny chat sessions (short prompt) while concurrently uploading 4 large multi-part embedding payloads (~500MB each) with default route priorities.
- Observe apigw connection queues and ingress prioritizer metrics; monitor serving-runtime memory and process restarts.

Logs / metrics collected:
- apigw metrics: per-tenant accept-queue depth, stream slot allocation, hedged-retry counts.
- prioritizer traces: long-tail allocation time for streaming routes, large-scale reassignments of slots during mixed bursts.
- serving-runtime logs: abrupt SIGABRT-like exits with thread-stack traces indicating memory pressure during KV cache operations.
- k8s events: pod OOMKill and rapidly successive restarts (~3 restarts within 2 minutes).
- dashboards: tenant-level 5xx spike, ingress priority share dropped to <2% for streaming traffic while embeddings consumed >95% of active slots.

Investigation notes:
- Initial hypothesis that embedding upload size alone triggered NVMe iowait was not supported: host disk metrics were within normal bounds and IO queue depth did not correlate strongly with crash windows.
- Observed that the ingress prioritizer assigned ephemeral slots aggressively to embedding routes when multipart upload flows established many concurrent sub-connections. This left near-zero minimum share for streaming routes for that tenant.
- The prioritizer algorithm allowed long-running batch flows to saturate the route slot pool because it did not enforce a minimum per-route share when tie-breaking among similar priority classes.
- When streaming traffic was starved, apigw queued streams and attempted hedged retries; the resulting connection churn amplified backend load, causing serving-runtime to allocate larger KV caches and then hit memory pressure leading to process exits.
- Root cause: ingress prioritizer bug that fails to enforce a configured "min-share" floor for streaming routes under mixed-workload tie conditions, enabling batch flows to monopolize ephemeral slots and drive a cascade of hedged retries and runtime restarts.

Mitigation / workaround applied:
- Support applied an immediate tenant-level burst throttle for embedding uploads at 02:30 UTC (reduced concurrent upload threads) which allowed streaming slot share to recover.
- Routing rule added to demote large embedding uploads to a lower-priority lane (noisy background) to prevent slot monopolization while a permanent fix was prepared.
- Customer advised to shard uploads into smaller pieces and schedule heavy backfills outside peak windows as a short-term operational mitigation.

Fix and rollout:
- Engineering implemented PR https://github.com/redwood-inference/ingress/pull/4582 which enforces a configurable min-share floor per route and improves tie-breaking to prefer round-robin among tenants within the same priority class.
- Patch was staged to canary in us-east-1 on 2026-03-11 10:00 UTC, validated with synthetic mixed-workload tests that mimic the reported pattern.
- Full prod rollout completed 2026-03-11 15:30 UTC. Monitoring showed tenant 5xx returned to baseline (~<0.5%) within 20 minutes post-rollout.

Resolution & follow-up:
- Status: Resolved. Root cause fixed and deployed; customer confirmed successful ingestion on follow-up call.
- Runbook action: add a new observability check to detect per-tenant slot monopolization and trigger automated demotion (safeguard) if a route's share falls below configured min-share for >30s. Ticket created: INT-4402 (internal) to add the safeguard.
- Engineering follow-ups: expose min-share thresholds in tenant configuration UI and document recommended settings for mixed workloads.

Notes for CS/SRE:
- If customers with mixed batch+stream workloads report elevated 5xx, check prioritizer "effective-share" metrics first and inspect concurrent sub-connection counts for multipart uploads.
- Short-term remediation steps: throttle tenant embedding concurrency and apply routing demotion; long-term: ensure min-share and rate-limits are tuned per tenant workload profile.
